_about: Shared petitions: the same ask, open in many places at once. County campaigns get one copy per county site, addressed to that county's own officials and counted toward its own goal; state campaigns get one copy per state; national ones a single copy. {county} and {state} are filled in. Posted by pipeline/campaigns.js (idempotent). 'hold' keeps a campaign from being posted until it's released.
started_by: Brayden Sanders, founder of County Commons

campaigns.title: Post every county payment online, every month, as searchable data
campaigns.why: Every check {county} writes is already a public record — but to see one, you have to file a request and wait. A monthly check register online (who was paid, how much, for what, from which fund) lets anyone follow the money without asking permission. Many counties and cities already do this. It costs little, because the county already keeps these records.

src.label: U.S. PIRG, Following the Money (state and local spending transparency)

best.name: Cook County, Illinois
best.rule: Cook County posts every payment to its vendors and other payees since December 1, 2016 as open data that you can download, with the check number, date, payee, amount and invoice numbers, and it publishes the data monthly.
best.label: Cook County Open Data, Check Register

best.name: DuPage County, Illinois
best.rule: The DuPage County Auditor posts a vendor expenditure report every month that lists each payment to vendors by name and date, with the accounting unit and account it was charged to, in a searchable format.
best.label: DuPage County Auditor, Vendor Expenditure Report

best.name: Oregon (state)
best.rule: Oregon law makes each county governing body publish, every month, a list of the last month's payments over $500, with who was paid, what for and how much, and it may be posted online.
best.label: Oregon Revised Statutes 294.250

ordinance.title: An ordinance to post every county payment online each month
sections: Residents should be able to see how {county} spends public money without filing a request.

Within 30 days after the end of each month, {county} shall post on its official website a list of every payment made from any county fund during that month. For each payment the list shall show the date, the payee, the amount, the fund and account charged, and a short description of what was purchased.

The list shall be posted as a searchable file, such as a spreadsheet, that anyone may read and download without a fee, registration or sign-in. Each month’s list shall stay online for at least five years.
Information that state or federal law makes confidential shall be withheld or redacted, and the list shall note where a redaction was made.
The ______________________ (office) is responsible for posting the list each month.

campaigns.title: Disclose every award paid from county tax money that's handed to outside groups
campaigns.why: Some county tax money goes to outside organizations — economic development corporations, nonprofits, districts — and once it leaves, the county's bidding and public-records rules may not follow it. We ask {county} to post, for every dollar passed through: who received it, how much, what for, and what was promised in return. Public money should stay traceable all the way to the last receipt.

campaigns.title: Before buying or renewing license-plate cameras: a public hearing, the contract posted, and a yearly audit
campaigns.why: License-plate cameras record every car that passes, not just suspects, and the data can be shared with other agencies and companies. Before {county} buys or renews any, we ask for a public hearing, the contract and data-sharing rules posted online, a limit on how long the data is kept, and a yearly public report of how often it was searched and why. This isn't for or against cameras — it's about rules everyone can see.

src.label: This county's page on cameras and plate readers

campaigns.title: Publish the jail's numbers every month
campaigns.why: The county jail is one of the biggest costs in the budget. We ask {county} to post a short monthly report: how many people were held, how many were awaiting trial, the average stay, and how many were held for the state or federal government. Counties that track these numbers can see what's driving costs — and many already share them.

src.label: Vera Institute, Incarceration Trends

campaigns.title: Text people a reminder before their court date
campaigns.why: Many missed court dates are simple forgetting — and a missed date can mean a warrant, an arrest and days in jail. In New York City, text reminders and a clearer court notice cut missed court dates by 21–26% in a randomized study, at very low cost. We ask {county}'s courts and clerk to text reminders before every court date.

src.label: J-PAL summary of Fishbane, Ouss and Shah, Science (2020)

campaigns.title: Post meeting agendas a week ahead, and video or minutes of every meeting, online
campaigns.why: Decisions about {county}'s money are made in public meetings, but working people can't always be there. We ask that every agenda be posted online at least a week before the meeting, with its supporting documents, and that video or full minutes of every meeting be posted afterward. If you can't attend, you should still be able to see what was decided and why.

campaigns.title: Require every county, city and school district in {state} to post its payments online
campaigns.why: Instead of a separate fight in every county, one state law can require every local government in {state} to post its check register online each month — who was paid, how much, and for what. The records already exist; this makes them easy to see.

src.label: U.S. PIRG, Following the Money

campaigns.title: Set statewide rules for license-plate camera data in {state}
campaigns.why: License-plate cameras are spreading fast, and the rules for their data differ town to town. We ask {state} lawmakers to set statewide limits: how long the data can be kept, who it can be shared with, a warrant or written reason to search it, and a yearly public report from every agency that uses it.

src.label: National Conference of State Legislatures, license-plate reader laws by state

campaigns.title: Make every {state} prison an accredited school for earning a living
campaigns.why: Nearly everyone in prison comes home. We ask {state} to make every prison an accredited place to learn — job training and education that end in a recognized credential, open to everyone held there. A RAND review of decades of studies found people who took part in prison education had 43% lower odds of returning to prison than those who didn't, and that it can save money by keeping people from coming back.

src.label: RAND, Evaluating the Effectiveness of Correctional Education (2013)

campaigns.title: Make every prison in America an accredited school for earning a living
campaigns.why: Nearly everyone in prison comes home. We ask Congress to require and fund accredited job training and education in every federal prison, and to help states do the same — training that ends in a recognized credential. A RAND review of decades of studies found people who took part in prison education had 43% lower odds of returning to prison than those who didn't.

src.label: RAND, Evaluating the Effectiveness of Correctional Education (2013)

campaigns.title: Keep calls from prison and jail affordable, and keep in-person visits
campaigns.why: Staying connected to family and friends is one of the best things for people inside and for the neighbors they come home to. A 2022 law passed with support from both parties let the FCC cap the price of prison and jail calls; the caps set in 2024 were raised in October 2025. We ask Congress and the FCC to keep calls affordable — and to keep in-person visits from being replaced by paid video.

src.label: FCC order FCC 25-75 (October 2025)
FCC, July 2024 rate-cap order

campaigns.title: Require project-by-project reporting of federal money sent to local governments
campaigns.why: Counties received $48.5 billion in federal pandemic relief. More than half was reported only as "revenue replacement," so the public can't trace it to what it bought. We ask Congress to require that federal money sent to local governments be reported project by project — what it paid for, who was paid, and what it delivered.

src.label: U.S. Treasury, State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds reporting

campaigns.title: Open unused county land to community gardens on a $1 revocable license
campaigns.why: Newark, New Jersey leases vacant lots to residents for $1 a year through its Adopt-a-Lot program, and Baltimore grants free, revocable licenses — neither sells the land. Brown County, Wisconsin has run community gardens through its Extension office since 1996: 13 gardens and 386 plots. We ask {county} to let residents garden unused county land under a simple revocable license.

src.label: Newark Adopt-a-Lot
Baltimore Adopt-a-Lot
UW–Madison Extension, Brown County community gardens

campaigns.title: Create a county food policy council with seats for growers, schools and the food bank
campaigns.why: A food policy council brings local government, growers, schools and food banks to one table. 283 were active in the U.S. as of 2020, according to a CDC journal study, and many are created by a local government resolution. We ask {county} to create one by resolution.

src.label: Preventing Chronic Disease (CDC), food policy councils
Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future

campaigns.title: Start a community seed library in the county library system
campaigns.why: Open-pollinated seed can be saved and replanted; hybrid seed does not come true from saved seed, and patented seed can’t legally be saved. A seed library lends seed at planting time and takes back a share at harvest. Seed Savers Exchange keeps a collection of more than 25,000 varieties. We ask {county} and its library to start one.

src.label: Seed Savers Exchange
University of Maryland Extension, saving seeds

campaigns.title: Set a goal for buying local food in county institutions, and ask school districts to do the same
campaigns.why: U.S. schools bought $789 million of local food in the 2013–14 school year, up 105% in two years, according to USDA. Districts with farm-to-school programs spent about 20% of their food budgets on local food (USDA 2019 Farm to School Census). We ask {county} to set a local-food buying goal for the jail and other county institutions, and to ask school districts to do the same.

src.label: USDA, 2016
USDA 2019 Farm to School Census

campaigns.title: Support a local food hub with shared cold storage and a commercial kitchen
campaigns.why: Food hubs collect produce from local farms and sell it to schools, hospitals and stores. In Michigan State University’s 2025 national survey, more than half of food hubs said grants made their sales to institutions possible. We ask {county} to support a food hub with shared cold storage and a commercial kitchen that local growers and food businesses can rent.

src.label: MSU 2025 National Food Hub Survey

campaigns.title: Support a local nonprofit’s application for a USDA Community Food Projects grant
campaigns.why: USDA’s Community Food Projects program funds local food projects up to $400,000, with a one-to-one match. Nonprofits apply, not counties — but county land, Extension staff time or a site can count toward the match. We ask {county} to offer a letter of support and an in-kind match to a local nonprofit that applies.

src.label: USDA NIFA, Community Food Projects

campaigns.title: Start an optional jail garden with the county Extension office
campaigns.why: In Smith County, Texas, people in the jail grow a garden and give all of the produce to the East Texas Food Bank — more than 160,000 pounds by the food bank CEO’s estimate. Garland County, Arkansas’s detention center works with the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture and donates produce to a food bank. We ask {county} to start an optional jail garden with its Extension office.

src.label: KETK, Smith County jail garden
Garland County Detention Center

campaigns.title: Include classroom, shop, kitchen and garden space in any new or renovated county jail
campaigns.why: A RAND review of decades of studies found that people who took part in education while locked up had 43% lower odds of returning to prison. In 2023, about 70% of people in U.S. jails had not been convicted of the charge they were held on (Bureau of Justice Statistics). We ask {county} to include classroom, trade-shop, kitchen and garden space in any new or renovated jail.

src.label: RAND, Correctional Education (2013)
BJS, Jail Inmates in 2023

campaigns.title: Pilot an optional, paid jail crew that builds homes with a licensed builder and a nonprofit
campaigns.why: Garland County, Arkansas’s jail runs a farm program, and Garland County Habitat for Humanity has built more than 170 homes since 1995. A federally funded review of studies found that vocational training in prison raised employment after release more than other education did. We ask {county} to pilot an optional, paid crew that builds homes alongside a licensed builder and a housing nonprofit.

src.label: Garland County Habitat for Humanity
Evaluating the Effectiveness of Correctional Education (meta-analysis)

campaigns.title: Fund a voluntary live-in program with housing, work and recovery that anyone may leave
campaigns.why: Bexar County, Texas runs a diversion center where people can choose treatment instead of jail. Job Corps is a federal live-in job-training program, rated in the Justice Department’s CrimeSolutions clearinghouse. We ask {county} to fund a voluntary live-in program with housing, paid work and recovery services that anyone may join or leave.

src.label: San Antonio Report, Bexar County diversion center
CrimeSolutions: Job Corps

campaigns.title: Receive resident petitions at a public meeting and post a written answer
campaigns.why: Stanford researchers found people who took part in deliberative polls followed politics more closely and voted more, nearly a year later. We ask {county}’s governing body to set a standing agenda time to receive petitions residents deliver, and to post a written answer to each one.

src.label: Stanford, lasting effects of deliberation

best.name: Framingham, Massachusetts
best.rule: If 100 voters sign a petition asking for a law, the city council or school committee must hold a public hearing and must respond to the petitioners within 30 days after the hearing.
best.label: Framingham Home Rule Charter (2025 edition), Article VIII, Section 1(b)

best.name: Clark County, Washington
best.rule: If voters equal to 3 percent of the county's last governor's race turnout sign a petition proposing a county law, the county council must hold a public hearing within 60 days and then pass, reject or change it within 30 days.
best.label: Clark County Home Rule Charter, Section 7.3 (Mini-initiative)

best.name: Gloucestershire County Council, England
best.rule: The council confirms a petition within 5 working days and sends the organizer a written response within 20 working days, and a petition with 5,000 signatures is debated at a full council meeting, where the organizer gets 5 minutes to present it.
best.label: Gloucestershire County Council: What will the council do when it receives my petition?

best.name: Edinburgh, Scotland
best.rule: A petition signed by 200 local voters (or 50 for a local issue) goes to a council committee, where the organizer may be invited to speak, and the council tells the organizer its decision in writing within 10 working days.
best.label: City of Edinburgh Council: Submitting a petition (petitions guidance)

best.name: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania
best.rule: If 25 city voters sign a petition and say they will attend, city council must hold a public hearing on the topic, and on pending legislation it cannot vote until that hearing is held.
best.label: Pittsburgh Home Rule Charter, Section 320 (City Clerk, June 2026 edition)

best.name: UK Parliament
best.rule: A petition with 10,000 signatures gets a written response from the UK Government, and a petition with 100,000 signatures is considered for a debate in Parliament.
best.label: UK Parliament petitions: How petitions work

best.name: Taiwan (national agencies)
best.rule: A proposal that gets 5,000 signatures within 60 days must get an answer from the national agency in charge within 2 months, and the agency can take up to 2 more months only if it posts the reason.
best.label: Directions for Implementing Online Participation in Public Policy (Executive Yuan / NDC), points 7 and 8

best.name: Reykjavík, Iceland
best.rule: In 2019, city rules said that each month the top 5 ideas with at least 25 votes and less than one year old, plus the top idea in each of 13 topic areas, go to the city committee in charge, which should take them up within a month.
best.label: City of Reykjavík working group report on democracy projects, November 2019 (section 3, 'Þín rödd í ráðum borgarinnar')

ordinance.title: An ordinance to receive resident petitions and answer them in writing
sections: Residents of {county} should know that a petition they deliver will be received in public and answered.
At each regular meeting, the {body} shall set aside time to receive petitions from residents of {county}.

Within 30 days after receiving a petition signed by at least ______ residents of {county}, the {body} shall send a written answer to the petition’s organizer and post it on the county’s official website.
Each petition received, and its answer, shall stay on the county’s website for at least five years.

campaigns.title: Hold a public hearing on how the general fund is divided before the budget is adopted
campaigns.why: Some county money is set aside by law for one purpose — roads, 911, libraries. The general fund is the part the county’s governing body divides each year. We ask {county} to hold a public hearing on how the general fund is divided before it adopts the budget.

src.label: This county’s money trail

campaigns.title: Direct {state} Medicaid to cover produce prescriptions
campaigns.why: Several states have federal approval to use Medicaid for nutrition support, according to KFF. A peer-reviewed study of 9 produce-prescription programs at 22 sites, with 3,881 participants, found people ate about one more serving of fruits and vegetables a day and had lower blood pressure, body weight and blood sugar, and less food insecurity. We ask {state} lawmakers and the governor to have the state Medicaid program cover produce prescriptions.

src.label: KFF, Section 1115 waiver watch
Produce prescription evaluation (2023)

campaigns.title: Require {state} agencies to publish purchase-card spending item by item
campaigns.why: Oklahoma posts its state purchase-card transactions online, searchable by merchant and item and updated monthly. Ohio’s OhioCheckbook put state transactions online. A U.S. Government Accountability Office review found 41–48% of sampled federal purchase-card transactions failed basic controls. We ask {state} lawmakers to require state agencies to publish purchase-card spending item by item.

src.label: Oklahoma purchase-card data

campaigns.title: Require federal agencies to publish government purchase-card spending item by item
campaigns.why: Federal purchase cards carried $39.4 billion across about 82 million transactions in fiscal 2025, according to the General Services Administration, and the card networks record each purchase’s merchant, category and amount. GSA publishes totals. We ask Congress to require agencies to publish the transactions themselves.

src.label: GSA SmartPay statistics

campaigns.title: Post the full county budget online every year, office by office and line by line
campaigns.why: {county}’s budget decides how its tax money is spent. We ask {county} to post its adopted budget online every year as searchable text, showing each office and what its money buys — salaries, supplies, contracts — so anyone can read it without filing a request.

src.label: International Budget Partnership, Open Budget Survey
County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Post the proposed budget online at least two weeks before the vote
campaigns.why: People can only weigh in on a budget they can see. The Open Budget Survey counts publishing the proposed budget before lawmakers vote as a basic part of budget openness. We ask {county} to post its proposed budget online at least two weeks before the vote, with the date and place of the public hearing.

src.label: International Budget Partnership, Open Budget Survey
County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Publish a short, plain-language guide to the county budget each year
campaigns.why: A budget book can run hundreds of pages. The Open Budget Survey counts a “citizens budget” — a short version in everyday words — as one of eight key budget documents. We ask {county} to publish one each year: where the money comes from, where it goes, and what changed.

src.label: International Budget Partnership, Open Budget Survey
County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Post the annual financial report and audit online, and keep five years up
campaigns.why: A budget is the plan; the annual financial report and audit show what really happened — every source of money, what was spent, what the county owes and what it has promised retirees. We ask {county} to post its annual financial report and audit online each year and keep at least five years posted. The Texas Comptroller’s Transparency Stars program asks for five years of trends.

src.label: Texas Comptroller, Transparency Stars
County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Post a monthly report of spending so far compared with the budget
campaigns.why: Most county governing bodies already see a monthly report of what has been spent against the budget. The Open Budget Survey counts reports during the year as a key budget document. We ask {county} to post that report online every month, so residents can see the same numbers.

src.label: International Budget Partnership, Open Budget Survey
County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Post budget and spending numbers as spreadsheets anyone can download
campaigns.why: A scanned page can be read but not searched, added up or compared. Checkbook NYC offers New York City’s budget, spending, contracts and payroll as downloadable data. We ask {county} to post its budget and spending numbers as spreadsheets or a data feed, free to download with no sign-in.

src.label: Checkbook NYC, New York City Comptroller
County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Post county credit-card and purchasing-card spending, item by item, every quarter
campaigns.why: County credit and purchasing cards are handy, and they’re public money. England’s councils must post their purchasing-card transactions at least every three months under their Transparency Code. We ask {county} to post every card purchase — date, merchant, amount and office — every quarter.

src.label: Local Government Transparency Code 2015 (England)
County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Post every county contract online, with the company, the amount and the contract itself
campaigns.why: Contracts are where much of the county’s money goes. England’s councils must post every contract and tender over £5,000. We ask {county} to post every contract award online — the company, the amount, what it buys — and the signed contract itself.

src.label: Local Government Transparency Code 2015 (England)
County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Post what every county job pays
campaigns.why: Pay is the biggest part of most county budgets. We ask {county} to post the pay or pay range for every job title each year, so residents can see what the county pays for the work it does.

src.label: Checkbook NYC, New York City Comptroller
County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Post every tax break and economic development deal: who got it, how much, and what they promised
campaigns.why: When a county gives a tax break or an incentive, it gives up money it would otherwise collect. The Texas Comptroller’s Transparency Stars program asks local governments to post their economic development deals. We ask {county} to post every tax abatement and incentive agreement — the company, the value, and the jobs or investment promised — and whether the promises were kept.

src.label: Texas Comptroller, Transparency Stars
County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Post the invoice behind every county payment
campaigns.why: A payment list says who was paid. The invoice says what for. County Commons hasn’t found any government that posts the invoice behind every payment yet. We ask {county} to be among the first: post the invoice or receipt with each payment, with personal details removed.

src.label: County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Record and post how each member votes on every motion
campaigns.why: “The motion carried” doesn’t tell residents how their own representative voted. We ask {county}’s governing body to record each member’s vote on every motion in its minutes and post them online.

src.label: County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Post a public log of records requests and how each was answered
campaigns.why: Records requests show what residents want to know, and a public log lets others find what was already released. Garland County, Arkansas posts every request and its status on a public portal. We ask {county} to post a log of every public records request — the date, what was asked, and how and when it was answered — with requesters’ personal details removed.

src.label: Garland County, Arkansas public records portal
County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Post every elected county official’s required financial disclosure filing online
campaigns.why: Elected officials already file financial disclosure forms by law; many sit on paper in an office. We ask {county} to post every elected county official’s required filing online each year, for every office alike, so anyone can read them without a trip to the courthouse.

src.label: County Commons transparency meter: the standard

campaigns.title: Before any data center is approved in {county}: a public hearing, its water and power use posted, any tax deal posted, and a binding limit on water use
campaigns.why: Data centers are being proposed in counties across the country, and they use a lot of electricity: the U.S. Department of Energy reports they used about 4.4% of all U.S. electricity in 2023 and may use 6.7% to 12% by 2028. Whether {county} wants one is for residents and their elected officials to decide. Either way, people should know before the vote how much water and power a project will use, what tax breaks it would get, and what limits it agrees to, and have a public hearing to say so.

src.label: U.S. Department of Energy, report on electricity demand from data centers (Dec. 20, 2024)

best.name: Loudoun County, Virginia
best.rule: Since March 18, 2025, a data center in Loudoun's Industrial Park, General Industry and Mineral Resources-Heavy Industry zones needs a special exception from the Board of Supervisors, so it can no longer be built by right.
best.label: Loudoun County, ZOAM-2024-0001 (Data Center Standards and Locations, Phase 1)

best.name: Tucson, Arizona
best.rule: Since September 4, 2026, a large data center in Tucson can only be built through a rezoning or planned-area change that the Mayor and Council decide at a public hearing, and it must show it has enough water and power and disclose its energy mix; a separate 2025 ordinance makes any user expected to take 10,000 CCF (about 7.48 million gallons) of water a month or more get its water conservation plan approved by the Mayor and Council.
best.label: City of Tucson, large-scale data center code amendment (adopted August 5, 2026)

best.name: Utah (state)
best.rule: Since July 1, 2026, a new Utah data center over 10,000 square feet that plans to use 75 acre-feet of water or more a year must report its expected water use before it is built and its real use every year, and the state posts those reports online by September 1.
best.label: Utah Division of Water Rights, HB 76 (2026) Data Center Water Transparency

best.name: Idaho (state)
best.rule: Since July 1, 2026, a new Idaho data center may not use water for cooling as a consumptive use unless a city, water district, or water and sewer district system supplies it.
best.label: Idaho Legislature, H0895 (2026), Idaho Code 42-252

ordinance.title: An ordinance setting conditions before any data center is approved
sections: “Data center” means a facility used mainly to house computer servers and related equipment for storing or processing data, with a planned peak electric demand of ______ megawatts or more.
No permit, rezoning, tax incentive or other approval by {county} for a data center shall be granted until the {body} holds a public hearing, with at least ______ days’ published notice.

At least ______ days before the hearing, the applicant shall file, and the county shall post on its official website, the facility’s expected annual and peak daily water use and the source of that water; its expected peak electric demand and annual electricity use, and the utility that will serve it; and its cooling method.

Any proposed tax abatement, payment in lieu of taxes, bond financing or other incentive for the facility, with its value and term and the jobs and investment promised, shall be posted at the same time.

Any approval shall set a binding limit on the facility’s water use of ______ gallons per day and require the operator to report its actual water and electricity use to the county each year, to be posted on the county’s website. Using more water than the limit is a violation of the approval.

campaigns.title: Post the test results and violations of every water system in {county} online, with the plan to fix each one
campaigns.why: Every community water system already tests its water, reports to the state, and must send customers a yearly water quality report. But results are spread across systems and state databases most people never see. One county page that links each system’s latest report and any violation, with what is being done to fix it, lets every household check its water in a minute.

src.label: U.S. EPA, Consumer Confidence Reports (annual water quality reports)
U.S. EPA, Safe Drinking Water Information System

best.name: Oregon (state)
best.rule: Oregon's drinking water office runs a live public site that lists every public water system with its test results, violations, public notices and enforcement orders, and you can filter the enforcement list by county.
best.label: Oregon Health Authority, Drinking Water Data Online

best.name: New York (state)
best.rule: New York's health department posts a yearly violation report for each county that names every water system with a violation, the contaminant, the months covered and whether it was fixed; Albany County's 2024 report lists 36 systems.
best.label: NY State Dept. of Health, 2024 Violation Summary by county

best.name: California (state)
best.rule: California's SAFER dashboard lists every failing water system, which you can filter by county, along with how much state help or funding it has received since 2017; 406 systems serving 645,279 people were on the failing list in the 2026 needs assessment.
best.label: California State Water Resources Control Board, SAFER Dashboard

ordinance.title: An ordinance to post drinking water results for every water system in the county
sections: Every household in {county} should be able to check its drinking water in one place.

{county} shall keep a page on its official website that lists each community water system serving county residents. For each system the page shall show a link to its most recent annual water quality report, a link to its record in the state drinking water database, and each violation the state reported in the past three years, with its status.

For each violation that is not resolved, the page shall show the corrective action and expected completion date reported by the water system or the state, when that information is available. The county shall ask each system for this information in writing every three months.
The page shall be updated at least every three months.
The ______________________ (office) is responsible for keeping the page current.

campaigns.title: Post every grant {county} applies for, wins and spends, with the project and what it got done
campaigns.why: Grants pay for roads, water lines, emergency services and much more, and they bring money home without raising local taxes. USAspending.gov lists federal awards by place, but not what each project achieved, and grants a county applied for and didn’t win aren’t listed anywhere. A public list of every application, award and result shows what the county is going after, and what the money built.

src.label: USAspending.gov, federal awards by place
Grants.gov, open federal grants

best.name: Orange County, California
best.rule: County policy says the Board of Supervisors must approve every grant application before it goes out, so a grants report at Board meetings lists each application and award, naming the department, the grant, the funder and the dollar amount.
best.label: County of Orange, Report on Grant Applications/Awards (April 28, 2026)

best.name: San Diego, California
best.rule: San Diego posts a yearly citywide grants report that lists every grant the city applied for and won; in fiscal year 2026 it sent 99 applications worth $418,165,400 and won 45 awards worth $175,472,086.
best.label: City of San Diego, FY26 Citywide Grants Report

best.name: Washington County, Oregon
best.rule: Washington County posts an ARPA projects dashboard and yearly reports for its $117 million in federal recovery money, which show its projects, spending and outcomes.
best.label: Washington County, ARPA (SLFRF) page and dashboard

ordinance.title: An ordinance to post every grant the county applies for, receives and spends
sections: Residents should be able to see what grants {county} is seeking, what it wins, and what the money accomplishes.
Within 30 days after submitting a grant application, {county} shall post on its official website the funder, the program, the amount requested, the project, and the county office that applied.
Within 30 days after learning that an application was awarded or denied, the county shall post the decision and the amount awarded.

For each grant awarded, the county shall post the amount spent at least every three months and, when the grant ends, a short report of what the project accomplished, including any results reported to the funder.
The list shall be searchable, free to read and download, and kept online for at least five years.
The ______________________ (office) is responsible for keeping the list current.
